title: Integration begins with a derivative
lead: Look for the function whose rate of change you have been given.
ideas: If $F\prime(x)=f(x)$, then $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$. For instance, $x^3$, $x^3+4$ and $x^3-9$ all have derivative $3x^2$. An indefinite integral records this whole family: $$\int f(x)\,dx=F(x)+C.$$ The constant is determined only when an extra value is given.

An integral with limits is different: $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is accumulated signed change. If a rate is below zero, its contribution is negative. A definite integral is a number; an indefinite integral is a family of functions.
Linearity is useful: $\int(af+bg)=a\int f+b\int g$. Integration does not distribute over products or quotients. Choose a method after simplifying the integrand.
trap: Do not write $\int_a^b f=F(b)+C$. The same constant cancels from $F(b)-F(a)$.

types.title: Find a curve from its gradient
types.question: The gradient of a curve at any point $(x,y)$ is $2x+3$. The curve passes through $(1,\,2)$. Find its equation.

title: Build a reliable formula bank
lead: Every standard integral is a differentiation rule read backwards.
ideas: Power rule: increase the power by one, then divide by the new power. $$\int x^n\,dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C,\qquad n\ne-1.$$ This rule cannot be used when $n=-1$, because the denominator would be zero.
Reciprocal rule: $$\int\frac{1}{x}\,dx=\ln|x|+C,\qquad x\ne0.$$ Use this on an interval that does not contain zero.
Exponential rule: $$\int e^{ax}\,dx=\frac{e^{ax}}{a}+C,\qquad a\ne0.$$ Differentiating $e^{ax}$ introduces a factor of $a$, so integration divides by $a$.
For a positive base other than one: $$\int b^x\,dx=\frac{b^x}{\ln b}+C,\qquad b>0,\ b\ne1.$$

Trigonometric rules: $$\begin{aligned}\int\sin x\,dx&=-\cos x+C\\[8pt]\int\cos x\,dx&=\sin x+C\\[8pt]\int\sec^2x\,dx&=\tan x+C\\[8pt]\int\csc^2x\,dx&=-\cot x+C\\[8pt]\int\sec x\tan x\,dx&=\sec x+C\\[8pt]\int\csc x\cot x\,dx&=-\csc x+C\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\int\tan x\,dx&=-\ln|\cos x|+C\\\int\cot x\,dx&=\ln|\sin x|+C\\\int\sec x\,dx&=\ln|\sec x+\tan x|+C\\\int\csc x\,dx&=\ln|\csc x-\cot x|+C\end{aligned}$$ Work on an interval without a pole. For a linear inner expression $ax+b$, divide the antiderivative by $a$.
Inverse-tangent form, for $a>0$: $$\int\frac{1}{a^2+x^2}\,dx=\frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)+C.$$
Inverse-sine form, for $a>0$: $$\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}\,dx=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)+C.$$ Its derivative is finite for $|x|<a$.
trap: The coefficient in $\int \frac{dx}{a^2+x^2}$ is $\frac{1}{a}$, not $\frac{1}{a^2}$.
answer: $\frac32e^{2x}+\frac15\sin5x+C$.

types.title: Divide by a power of x
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^3+5x^2-4}{x^2}\,dx$.
types.type: Divide, then use the power rule

types.title: Use an identity to remove a square
types.question: Evaluate $\int\tan^2x\,dx$.

title: Substitution: recognise the inner derivative
lead: A good substitution removes complexity from both the expression and its differential.
ideas: The chain rule says $\frac{d}{dx}F(g(x))=F\prime(g(x))g\prime(x)$. Reverse it: $$\int f(g(x))g\prime(x)\,dx=\int f(u)\,du,\qquad u=g(x).$$ Write $du$ explicitly. If only a constant factor is missing, compensate for that factor outside the integral.

Three useful signals are $\frac{f\prime}{f}$, $f\prime\,f^n$ and $\frac{f\prime}{\sqrt{f}}$. They lead to $\ln|f|$, $\frac{f^{n+1}}{n+1}$ and $2\sqrt f$, respectively. The first formula requires $f\ne0$.
For a definite integral, change the bounds at the same time. You may keep the new variable throughout; there is no need to substitute back before evaluating.

examples.title: A derivative hidden in the numerator
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{4x+3}{2x^2+3x+7}\,dx$.

trap: After changing to $u$, do not use the old $x$-bounds on an antiderivative in $u$.

types.title: A linear expression inside a power
types.question: Evaluate $\int(3x-2)^5\,dx$.

types.title: An exponential with an inverse function
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{e^{\tan^{-1}x}}{1+x^2}\,dx$.

types.title: Derive the rule for tan x
types.question: Show that $\int\tan x\,dx=\ln|\sec x|+C$.

title: Rational functions: divide, factor, decompose
lead: The denominator tells you which simpler fractions are possible.
ideas: If the numerator degree is at least the denominator degree, divide first. For distinct linear factors use $\frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{x-b}$. A repeated factor $(x-a)^m$ needs every power from $1$ to $m$. An irreducible quadratic needs a linear numerator.

After clearing denominators, compare coefficients or substitute convenient values. For a quadratic denominator, try writing the numerator as a multiple of its derivative plus a constant; complete the square for the leftover part.

examples.title: A quadratic that does not factor over the reals
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{3x+8}{x^2+4x+8}\,dx$.

trap: For $(x+1)^2$, writing only $\frac{A}{(x+1)^2}$ loses a necessary term.
answer: Divide to get $1+\frac{2}{x^2+1}$. The result is $x+2\tan^{-1}x+C$.

title: Integration by parts: make the next integral easier
lead: Choose the factor that becomes simpler when differentiated.
ideas: From $(uv)\prime=u\prime v+uv\prime$, $$\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du.$$ Choose a differentiable $u$ and a $dv$ you can actually integrate. A memory aid about the order of functions is only a starting point; judge the integral that remains.
For powers of $x$ multiplied by an exponential or sine/cosine, repeat parts until the polynomial disappears. Some integrals return to the original integral; collect those terms algebraically.
trap: The minus sign in $uv-\int v\,du$ is essential; a negative derivative can then turn that subtraction into addition.
answer: Parts gives $[\frac{x^2\ln x}{2}-\frac{x^2}{4}]_1^e=\frac{e^2+1}{4}$.

title: Trigonometric powers and rationalisation
lead: Use identities to create a substitution, rather than expanding blindly.
ideas: For $\sin^m x\cos^n x$, save a cosine factor if $n$ is odd and use $u=\sin x$; save a sine factor if $m$ is odd and use $u=\cos x$. If both powers are even, half-angle identities reduce them.

For a rational expression in $\sin x$ and $\cos x$, $t=\tan (\frac{x}{2})$ gives $\sin x=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}$, $\cos x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$ and $dx=\frac{2dt}{1+t^2}$. It is a general method, but a simpler substitution should be preferred when available.
In a definite integral, split the interval if the chosen tangent substitution has a pole inside it. Algebraic cancellation must not hide a discontinuity.
trap: An identity such as $\sqrt{\cos^2x}=\cos x$ is false when $\cos x<0$; the root is $|\cos x|$.
answer: Use $\frac{1-\cos 4x}{2}$: $\frac{x}{2}-\frac{\sin 4x}{8}+C$.

title: Radicals and standard algebraic forms
lead: Choose a substitution that turns the root into a familiar identity.
ideas: For $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$, use $x=a\sin\theta$ with a range where $\cos\theta\ge0$. For $\sqrt{x^2+a^2}$, use $x=a\tan\theta$. For $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$, a secant substitution works on a suitable interval.

Useful results, for $a>0$, are $$\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}=\ln|x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}|+C,$$ $$\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}=\ln|x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}|+C,$$ and $$\int\frac{dx}{x^2-a^2}=\frac1{2a}\ln\left|\frac{x-a}{x+a}\right|+C.$$ Respect the real domain and avoid the poles.
Completing the square connects a general quadratic radical to these forms. For a numerator $px+q$, separate a multiple of the derivative of the quadratic before making a more elaborate substitution.
trap: Carry the transformed $dx$ through the substitution; replacing just the radical is not enough.
answer: With $u=x+2$, the answer is $\sin^{-1} (\frac{x+2}{4})+C$, for $|x+2|<4$.

types.title: Complete the square under a root
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+2x+2}}$.

types.title: A linear numerator over a root
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{x^2+2x+3}}\,dx$.

title: Definite integrals: accumulation and the fundamental theorem
lead: The area picture explains both the signs and the endpoint subtraction.
ideas: For continuous $f$, let $A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)dt$. A small increase $h$ adds a thin strip with approximate signed area $f(x)h$. Taking the limit gives $A\prime(x)=f(x)$.
If $F\prime=f$, then $A-F$ has derivative zero; evaluate at $a$ to obtain $$\int_a^b f(x)dx=F(b)-F(a).$$ Also $\int_a^b f=-\int_b^a f$ and $\int_a^b f+\int_b^c f=\int_a^c f$.
Geometric area uses $\int_a^b|f(x)|dx$. Signed accumulation uses $\int_a^b f(x)dx$. These agree only when the integrand is nonnegative throughout the interval.

examples.title: A zero integral can hide nonzero area
examples.question: Compare $\displaystyle\int_0^2(x-1)\,dx$ with $\displaystyle\int_0^2|x-1|\,dx$.

examples.title: Do not integrate through a pole
examples.question: Why is $\left[-\dfrac{1}{x}\right]_{-1}^1=-2$ not the value of $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1 \frac{dx}{x^2}$?
steps: $\dfrac1{x^2}$ is not continuous at $x=0\in[-1,1]$, so $F(b)-F(a)$ cannot be used.

trap: Continuity is a sufficient hypothesis for the form of the fundamental theorem used here. Check it before using the formula mechanically.
answer: $A(2)=0$ because its bounds coincide; $A\prime(2)=2^2+1=5$.

types.title: Direct use of the fundamental theorem
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^2\left(4x^3-5x^2+6x+9\right)dx$.

title: Reflection: make two difficult integrands add to something simple
lead: Before searching for an antiderivative, compare the integrand with its mirror image.
ideas: The substitution $x=a+b-t$ proves $$\int_a^b f(x)dx=\int_a^b f(a+b-x)dx.$$ The reversed limits and negative differential cancel. If the sum of the two integrands simplifies, add the two expressions for the same integral.

On $[0,a]$, if $f(a-x)=f(x)$, then $$\int_0^a xf(x)dx=\frac a2\int_0^a f(x)dx.$$ Proof: reflection changes $x$ to $a-x$ while leaving $f$ unchanged; add the two forms. More generally, split any weight into a symmetric part and an antisymmetric part about $\frac{a}{2}$.
A common pattern is $\frac{h(x)}{h(x)+h(a-x)}$ with a nonzero denominator: its integral is $\frac{a}{2}$. For sine and cosine on $[0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$, reflection interchanges the two functions.

examples.title: A high power that does not need expansion
examples.question: Evaluate $I=\displaystyle\int_0^4 \frac{(x+2)^5}{(x+2)^5+(6-x)^5}\,dx$.

trap: The weighted midpoint identity needs symmetry of $f$; it is not true for every integrand.
answer: Reflection interchanges numerator terms, giving twice the integral as $\frac{\pi}{2}$. Answer: $\frac{\pi}{4}$.

title: Parity, periodicity and weighted periods
lead: Translate the interval when the symmetry is not centred at zero.
ideas: If $f(-x)=-f(x)$, an integrable odd function has zero integral over $[-a,a]$. If $f(-x)=f(x)$, the integral is twice its value over $[0,a]$. A shift $u=x-c$ reveals symmetry about $x=c$.
For an integrable function of period $T$, every interval of length $T$ has the same integral, and $\int_0^{nT}f=n\int_0^T f$. Split the interval into complete periods and a remainder.

For a weighted periodic integral, let $A=\int_0^T f(t)dt$ and $B=\int_0^T tf(t)dt$. In the $k$th period use $x=t+kT$. Summing gives $$\int_0^{nT}xf(x)dx=nB+\frac{Tn(n-1)}2A.$$ The weight itself is not periodic.
trap: An odd function with a nonintegrable singularity does not automatically have an integral of zero.
answer: The period is $\pi$ and one-period integral is $2$. Thus the answer is $8$.

types.title: An odd power over a symmetric interval
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-\frac\pi2}^{\frac\pi2}\sin^7x\,dx$.

types.title: Separate odd and even parts
types.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-\frac\pi2}^{\frac\pi2}\left(x^3+x\cos x+\tan^5x+1\right)dx$.
steps: $x^3,\ x\cos x,\ \tan^5x$ are odd $\Rightarrow$ their integrals are $0$

title: Modulus, floor and fractional part
lead: Split exactly where the formula changes.
ideas: For $|g(x)|$, locate all zeros of $g$ in the interval, make a sign chart, and integrate the correct signed expression on each subinterval. For $\lfloor g(x)\rfloor$, split where $g(x)$ crosses an integer.
The fractional part is $\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor$. On $[k,k+1)$, use $x=k+t$ so that $\{x\}=t$. A value at an isolated endpoint does not change a Riemann integral.
Do not replace $\lfloor x^2\rfloor$ by $(\lfloor x\rfloor)^2$. The breakpoints of the former occur at square roots of integers.

examples.title: A floor function inside a product
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^2x\lfloor x^2\rfloor\,dx$.

trap: For a nonmonotone inner function, the same integer may be crossed more than once. Find every breakpoint.

title: Riemann sums: read the width and the sample point
lead: A sum becomes an integral only after its scaling is identified.
ideas: For continuous $f$ on $[a,b]$, $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{b-a}{n}\sum_{r=1}^n f\left(a+\frac{(b-a)r}{n}\right)=\int_a^b f(x)dx.$$ Left endpoints and midpoint samples have the same limit. The factor $\frac{b-a}{n}$ is the strip width.
In rational sums, divide each occurrence of $r$ by $n$ and factor out the matching power of $n$. Check that one overall factor $\frac{1}{n}$ remains. Missing this factor changes the limit completely.

Finite products can be handled by logarithms when all factors are positive. A product of many factors close to $1$ often becomes an exponential of an integral; justify the approximation uniformly over the samples.
trap: Not every expression containing a sum is a Riemann sum. Establish both the sample points and their width.
answer: The limit is $\int_0^1\sqrt{1+3x}dx=\frac{14}{9}$.

title: Variable limits, integral equations and local behaviour
lead: Differentiate the accumulated quantity before trying to evaluate it.
ideas: For continuous $f$ and differentiable bounds, $$\frac d{dx}\int_{u(x)}^{v(x)}f(t)dt=f(v(x))v\prime(x)-f(u(x))u\prime(x).$$ Both endpoint chain-rule factors matter.

An equation defining $f$ through an integral may turn into a differential equation. After differentiating, retain the value obtained from the original equation at a convenient point; differentiation alone can lose that condition.
For $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)dt$, zeros of $f$ are stationary points of $F$. They are extrema only when $f$ changes sign. The sign chart is often more useful than an explicit formula for $F$.

examples.title: A stationary point without a turn
examples.question: For $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x(t-1)^2(t-3)\,dt$, classify the stationary points.

trap: The integration variable is a dummy variable; differentiate through the moving bounds, not by treating that dummy variable as $x$.
answer: Write $H=x\int_0^x(t^2+2)dt-\int_0^xt(t^2+2)dt$. Endpoint terms cancel in $H\prime$, so $H\prime\prime=x^2+2$ and the answer is $3$.

title: Inverse functions and composition
lead: A difficult inverse can disappear after changing the variable.
ideas: Let $g$ be continuously differentiable and strictly monotone on $[a,b]$. Substitution $y=g(x)$ and integration by parts give $$\int_{g(a)}^{g(b)}g^{-1}(y)dy=[xg(x)]_a^b-\int_a^b g(x)dx.$$ The oriented-limit form also works for a decreasing $g$.
For an integral of $f(g(x))g\prime(x)$, substitute $u=g(x)$ directly. The same idea works when $f$ is defined implicitly, or when $f$ itself is an accumulated integral.
trap: An inverse-function formula needs a one-to-one function on the selected interval; a globally nonmonotone function may still work on a suitable restricted interval.
answer: The boundary term is $3(8)-0(2)=24$. Subtract $14$ to obtain $10$.

title: Reduction formulae and beta-type integrals
lead: Relate the difficult integral to a simpler member of the same family.
ideas: Let $I_n=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sin^n xdx$. Integration by parts with $u=\sin^{n-1}x$ and $dv=\sin xdx$ gives $I_n=(n-1)(I_{n-2}-I_n)$ for integer $n\ge2$. Therefore $$I_n=\frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2},\qquad I_0=\frac{\pi}{2},\ I_1=1.$$

For nonnegative integers $m,n$, repeated parts gives $$\int_0^1x^m(1-x)^ndx=\frac{m!n!}{(m+n+1)!}.$$ To see the recurrence, integrate $(1-x)^n$ and differentiate $x^m$: $B_{m,n}=\frac{mB_{m-1,n+1}}{n+1}$ for $m\ge1$. Finish with $B_{0,k}=\frac{1}{k+1}$.
Reflection also gives $B_{m,n}=B_{n,m}$. This is a useful independent check and a quick way to choose the shorter reduction.
trap: Do not use the integer factorial formula for arbitrary real exponents without replacing factorials by the appropriate beta/gamma expressions and checking convergence.
answer: The integral is $\frac{1!4!}{6!}=\frac{1}{30}$, so the required value is $1$.

title: Inequalities and least possible values
lead: Sometimes a bound is the answer; an antiderivative is unnecessary.
ideas: If $m\le f\le M$ on $[a,b]$ with $a<b$, then $m(b-a)\le\int_a^bf\le M(b-a)$. Pointwise inequalities integrate in the same direction. If a continuous nonnegative function is positive somewhere, its integral is strictly positive.

Integrate a square: $\int(f-cg)^2\ge0$ for every real $c$. The discriminant of this quadratic in $c$ cannot be positive. This proves Cauchy–Schwarz: $$(\int_a^b fg)^2\le(\int_a^bf^2)(\int_a^bg^2).$$ Equality holds when the two functions are proportional (apart from sets of integral measure zero).
With $g=1$, $\int_a^b f^2\ge\frac{(\int_a^bf)^2}{b-a}$. Always test whether the equality function is allowed by every condition.

examples.title: A lower bound with an attainable equality
examples.question: Continuous $f$ on $[0,2]$ satisfies $\displaystyle\int_0^2f=8$. Find the least possible $\displaystyle\int_0^2f^2$.

examples.title: Two constraints require a better comparison
examples.question: Continuous $f$ on $[0,1]$ satisfies $\displaystyle\int_0^1f=0$ and $\displaystyle\int_0^1xf=2$. Find the least $\displaystyle\int_0^1f^2$.

trap: A numerical lower bound is not necessarily a minimum: you must show an admissible function attains equality.
check: For positive continuous $f$ on $[0,1]$ with $\int f=3$, prove $\int \frac{1}{f}\ge\frac{1}{3}$.
answer: Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to $\sqrt f$ and $\frac{1}{\sqrt f}$: $1\le(\int f)(\int\frac{1}{f})=3\int\frac{1}{f}$. Equality holds for $f=3$.

title: Parameters inside integrals
lead: A parameter can turn an awkward logarithm into a rational function.
ideas: If $f(x,a)$ and its partial derivative with respect to $a$ are continuous on a fixed compact rectangle, then $$\frac d{da}\int_u^v f(x,a)dx=\int_u^v\frac{\partial f}{\partial a}(x,a)dx.$$ This is a sufficient condition; improper endpoint cases require additional justification.
Use an easy parameter value to determine the integration constant after integrating back. A parameter method is not complete until that value is checked.
If endpoints also depend on the parameter, include their contributions as well as the integral of the partial derivative.

examples.title: A moving parameter and a moving endpoint
examples.question: Find $H'(a)$ for $H(a)=\displaystyle\int_0^a\ln(1+at)\,dt$, $a>0$.

trap: If you differentiate only the integrand when the bounds move, the endpoint terms are lost.
answer: Continuity permits differentiation under the integral. At $a=0$ the integrand is $x$, so the answer is $\frac{1}{2}$.

title: Logarithmic symmetry and improper endpoints
lead: A singular endpoint may still have a finite integral, but it must be handled as a limit.
ideas: Near zero, $\ln x$ diverges, yet $\int_0^1\ln xdx=-1$ because $x\ln x\to0$. By contrast, $\int_0^1\frac{dx}{x}$ diverges. A large value near an endpoint alone does not decide convergence.

To derive the log-sine result, put $L=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\ln (\sin x)dx$. Reflection gives the same value with cosine. Therefore $2L=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\ln (\sin 2x)dx-(\frac{\pi}{2})\ln 2$. Substituting $u=2x$ and reflecting on $[0,\pi]$ makes the first integral equal to $L$. Thus $$L=-\frac\pi2\ln2.$$ The logarithmic endpoint singularities are integrable, so these changes can be justified by truncated limits.
For a parameter $a>0$, $\ln(a\sin x)=\ln a+\ln(\sin x)$. This simple separation produces many exact values without inventing a new antiderivative.

examples.title: An improper integral with a symmetric weight
examples.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi x\ln(2\sin x)\,dx$.

trap: Do not apply a remembered log-sine or symmetry result to a different angle without checking the interval and transformed function.
answer: Split as $\ln\sin x-\ln\cos x$. The two convergent improper integrals agree by reflection, giving $0$.

title: Combine two ideas: a demanding problem is often two familiar steps
lead: Look for what can be simplified before committing to a long calculation.
ideas: A useful sequence is: check the domain; look for a symmetry; simplify the transformed sum; then choose a substitution or inequality. Several advanced questions become short only after the first structural observation.
When $f(x)+f(a-x)$ is known, you may determine an integral against a symmetric weight without determining $f$. If the weight is not symmetric, separate it into its reflected sum and difference first.

examples.title: A functional relation with a weight
examples.question: Continuous $f$ satisfies $f(x)+f(2-x)=x^2-2x+8$ on $[0,2]$. Find $I=\displaystyle\int_0^2(x-1)^2f(x)\,dx$.

examples.title: Minimise an integral with respect to a constant
examples.question: Find the minimum of $J(a)=\displaystyle\int_0^3(x^2-a)^2\,dx$ over real $a$.

trap: A long expression does not necessarily need a long antiderivative. First ask which part stays unchanged by reflection or substitution.
answer: The weight is symmetric. Twice the required integral is $6\int_{-2}^2u^2du=32$. The answer is $16$.

title: Limits involving accumulated functions
lead: Use the local behaviour of the integrand and keep the first nonzero term.
ideas: If $f$ is continuous at $a$, the average over a shrinking interval tends to $f(a)$: $\lim_{h\to0}\frac1h\int_a^{a+h}f(t)dt=f(a)$. This works from either side with oriented limits.

When the leading term vanishes, expand to the necessary order, or apply the fundamental theorem and L’Hôpital’s rule where its hypotheses hold. An expansion $f(t)=c t^m+o(t^m)$ near zero gives $\int_0^xf(t)dt=\frac{cx^{m+1}}{m+1}+o(x^{m+1})$ for integer $m\ge0$.

For two moving bounds near the same point, account for the difference of the corresponding powers. Do not replace a small integral by its width times a value that is itself zero without examining the next term.
trap: If the denominator vanishes to third order, a first-order approximation may be too weak to determine the limit.
answer: $\sin3t=3t+O(t^3)$ gives an integral $\frac{3x^2}{2}+O(x^4)$, hence $\frac{3}{2}$.

title: Recurrences, bounds and a limiting constant
lead: Two relations can determine an asymptotic value without an explicit formula.
ideas: Let $R_n=\int_0^1\frac{x^n}{1+x}dx$. The identity $\frac{x^n}{1+x}+\frac{x^{n+1}}{1+x}=x^n$ gives $R_n+R_{n+1}=\frac{1}{n+1}$. Since $0<x<1$, the sequence is positive and decreasing.

To find its scale, write $\frac{1}{1+x}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1-x}{2(1+x)}$. Then $$0\le R_n-\frac1{2(n+1)}\le\frac12\int_0^1x^n(1-x)dx=\frac1{2(n+1)(n+2)}.$$ Multiplication by $n+1$ and squeezing gives $(n+1)R_n\to\frac{1}{2}$.
This method explains why samples close to $x=1$ dominate: $x^n$ becomes small away from that endpoint. The coefficient is the endpoint value of the remaining continuous factor.

examples.title: Use a recurrence to avoid long division
examples.question: Find $R_3=\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x^3}{1+x}\,dx$.

trap: From $R_n+R_{n+1}\to0$ alone you cannot infer the value of $nR_n$; scaling needs a quantitative bound.
answer: The expression is $3+\frac{n+1}{n+2}$, so the limit is $4$.

title: Reciprocal substitutions on an infinite interval
lead: The transformation $x\mapsto\frac{1}{x}$ can exchange powers in the numerator.
ideas: In a convergent improper integral on $(0,\infty)$, $x=\frac{1}{t}$ changes $dx$ to $-\frac{dt}{t^2}$. Track both the differential and reversed limits. This can pair rational functions of $x$ and $\frac{1}{x}$.
An improper substitution can be justified on finite truncated intervals and then by taking limits. Establish convergence before combining the transformed expressions.
trap: The parameter condition is part of the result. An expression containing a square root is not proof that the original integral converges.
answer: Reciprocal substitution makes this equal to $I(7)$. The result is $\frac{\pi}{6}$.
